content: I have some projects that depend on batteries and require that precompileModules is set to true. This hasn't been a problem in the past, but updating to v4.31.0 yields now a build cycle error due to the batteries dependency. This problem is already documented in #1832, but I haven't seen any comments on the issue or any discussion of it on Zulip. Are there currently any plans or timetables for tackling this? I'm trying to figure out whether I should just wait to update my projects until this is resolved, or whether it will be necessary for me to try to remove my project's batteries dependency.
cc @Mac Malone Could you have a look when you have time? I just want to rule out a lake bug before working on this.

Thanks for bringing this up @Josh Clune! BatteriesRecycling is meant to be a transitional location. The modules there are intended to be moved to separate repos. The temporary circular dependency was intentional but not carefully tested. Could you point to one of your projects for investigation purposes? (DM is fine if you prefer.)
The project I was trying to update when I ran into this was Duper.

I should note though that the details of the downstream project are largely irrelevant. I get the same error when I create the following fresh project:

lean-toolchain:

leanprover/lean4:v4.31.0

lakefile.toml:

name = "BatteriesImport"
version = "0.1.0"
precompileModules = true
defaultTargets = ["BatteriesImport"]

[[require]]
name = "Batteries"
scope = "leanprover-community"
rev = "v4.31.0"

[[lean_lib]]
name = "BatteriesImport"

BatteriesImport.lean:

import Batteries

François G. Dorais said:

cc Mac Malone Could you have a look when you have time? I just want to rule out a lake bug before working on this.

This is expected. Libraries with precompiled modules cannot mutually depend on each other. This is because modules from different libaries are built into a single shared library and loaded together. This minmizes the number of libraries Lean needs to load with precompiled modules enabled (which can significantly impact performance).
